biggestGap: You cannot tell what any piece is by looking at it. From the play camera every piece is the same pale armoured figure seen from behind, and the only thing separating the types is height: measured through the app's live camera at 1280x800, the back rank renders rook 119.2 px, knight 132.2 px, bishop 141.1 px, queen 168.2 px, king 187.0 px, pawn 94.7 px. Rook to knight is 13.0 CSS px and knight to bishop is 8.8 CSS px — 7 to 11 percent of the piece's own height, on shapes with the same silhouette, the same pale stone and the same helmet. Nothing else distinguishes them: no colour, no crest, no base marking, no label. This is not a software-renderer artifact (though this box's 0.38x buffer shrinks those gaps to 4.9 and 3.3 actually-rendered pixels); at full 1920 px capture resolution through the same PLAY_SHOT the back rank still reads as eight interchangeable armoured torsos. The consequence is concrete: I chose every one of my nine moves by reading window.__WC__.game.state().fen out of the JS console, because looking at the board did not tell me where my knights were. Nothing surfaces the engine's move either — state.lastMove is maintained but the HUD in main.ts prints only turn, move number, CHECK, result and 'thinking…', so after the engine answers you cannot tell what it just played. A person has neither the FEN nor the move; they would have to click pieces one at a time and infer the type from the shape of the legal-move markers.
critiqueDetail:
It plays. Not 'accepts input' — plays. I drove the real canvas with my own Playwright script in interactive mode (no query parameters), projecting squares through window.__WC__.world.camera and clicking with page.mouse, and completed a nine-move game: 1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bc4 d5 4.d4 dxc4 5.Nc3 Nf6 6.O-O Bb4 7.Bg5 Bxc3 8.Qe2 Bxb2 9.Rad1 Nd4. Castling worked. Every position was replayed through a fresh Engine instance imported from /src/chess/index.ts: all nine legal, all nine an exact FEN round-trip, 28-35 legal replies each, result 'playing' throughout, zero page errors and zero console errors. tools/play-test.mjs also passes on its own — e2-e4 accepted, engine answered Nc6, no errors.

BOTH of round 2's findings are fixed, and I checked them specifically.

The back-rank crop is gone. interactive.ts now clamps the interactive frame to a 1.6:1 aspect instead of pinning it to the 2.39:1 capture letterbox, and because main.ts's fitFov holds the horizontal extent fixed, the narrower frame opens the vertical fov from 30 to 43.6 degrees — a taller view of the same board rather than a smaller one. Measured: on a 1280x800 canvas, rank 1 projects to y=680-683 with the canvas ending at 800, every square on-screen, and rank spacing at the near edge is 89 px (d1->d2) and 74 px (d2->d3) against the 22-28 px slivers of round 2. Rank 8 sits at y=283. The whole board is in the picture with margin above and below, exactly as PLAY_SHOT claims. I never once failed to click a back-rank piece.

The reply decay is gone. Real seconds from my move landing to the engine's move landing, across the game: 1.00, 1.04, 1.01, 1.00, 1.02, 1.00, 1.00, 1.00. Dead flat. Round 2 measured 1.14 rising to 36.46 as debris accumulated; this run went from 339 to 449 scene meshes over the same span and the reply time did not move by 40 ms. thinker.ts now runs the 60k-node search in a module worker and delivers the answer by callback rather than inside update(), and interactive.ts's `later()` fires on whichever of scene time or wall clock arrives first — so a slow renderer can no longer hold the game hostage. The residual ~1.0 s is a deliberate floor (MIN_THINK_MS 500 / SETTLE_MS 700), not latency.

Abuse did not break it. Clicking an empty square, clicking the engine's rook on a8, clicking the same knight twice, clicking 5,5 far off the board, clicking below the canvas at y=795, and clicking a2 then h6 as an illegal destination all left the FEN byte-identical and the turn unchanged. Spamming five clicks across the board while state.thinking was true also left the FEN unchanged, and the engine then answered normally and the game continued to move 10. The rAF loop never stopped and window.__WC__ was still present at the end.

The affordances are real and correct — this is the thing that makes it a game rather than a coordinate puzzle. I enumerated every visible mesh sitting just above the marble after each click: selecting the b1 knight lit exactly b1, a3, c3; selecting the e2 pawn lit exactly e2, e3, e4; clicking empty a5 lit exactly a5 as a refusal scorch. No false positives, no missing squares.

Captures resolve. Qxd5 took a pawn: the victim vanished from the FEN, scene meshes went 339 -> 425 (+86 debris meshes) within 6 real seconds of the click, and dust and rubble are visible on the marble in the screenshots. Round 2's complaint that debris was scheduled on world.time and arrived ~80x late is addressed by the same dual-deadline `later()`.

The honest caveat, unchanged: this box has no GPU. SwiftShader renders at 0.70 fps (1428 ms per frame) and the adaptive scaler sits on its lowest rung, a 486x304 buffer stretched to a 1280 px CSS canvas. world.time therefore advances at 0.035x the wall clock, so anything still specified as a duration in scene seconds — the walk from square to square, the strike, the recovery — is a slideshow. That is hardware. What is NOT hardware is the piece legibility above, which survives at full capture resolution.

The scripted path is NOT regressed, and is in fact bit-for-bit what it was in round 2. Two king-surrender captures at t=2.8 are byte-identical to each other AND carry round 2's exact md5, 45ebe28f78b6837bb2816b5fcccbe9ab at 2,264,723 bytes — so the play-camera work touched nothing the capture harness renders. tools/verify-mate.mjs reports all three lines ending in a real verified checkmate: wreckage 21 plies / 9 captures / Qxc8#, strike 7 plies / Qxf7#, scholar 7 plies / Qxf7#, each replayLegal, fenMatch, inCheck=true and legalReplies=0.
metrics: 9 full moves played through the real canvas, all positions legal + FEN round-trip exact, 28-35 legal replies each, 0 page errors, 0 console errors. Engine reply (real s): 1.00, 1.04, 1.01, 1.00, 1.02, 1.00, 1.00, 1.00 — flat while scene meshes went 339 -> 449. Click-to-accept 0.36-0.39 s (two outliers at 1.03 and 4.12 s). Rank 1 at y=680-683 on an 800 px canvas, all squares on-screen, rank spacing 89/74 px; rank 8 at y=283; frame aspect 1.600, fov 43.6. Renderer 0.70 fps / 1428 ms per frame, buffer 486x304 behind 1280 px CSS (0.38x rung); world.time runs at 0.035x wall clock. Capture Qxd5: victim gone, meshes 339 -> 425 (+86) within 6 real s. Affordances exact: b1 -> {b1,a3,c3}, e2 -> {e2,e3,e4}, empty a5 -> {a5} refusal. Six abuse cases + a 5-click spam during the engine's turn: FEN unchanged in every one, game recovered and continued. Piece height on screen: pawn 94.7, rook 119.2, knight 132.2, bishop 141.1, queen 168.2, king 187.0 CSS px; rook->knight 13.0 px, knight->bishop 8.8 px (4.9 and 3.3 actually-rendered px at this box's 0.38x). Scripted: cmp byte-identical, md5 45ebe28f78b6837bb2816b5fcccbe9ab — same as round 2; verify-mate 3/3 real checkmates, 0 legal replies each.

history.gap: none — 3/3 demo lines verified as real checkmate with zero legal replies

The play camera crops White's own back rank off the bottom of the frame — all eight rank-1 square centres sit 20-23 px below the canvas edge, leaving a 22-28 px sliver, so clicking where your own knight or king appears to be does nothing. Deterministic at every window size, and it hits on move 2.

You cannot tell what any piece is by looking at it. Every piece is the same pale armoured figure from behind and only height separates the types: rook 119.2 px, knight 132.2 px, bishop 141.1 px on screen — 13.0 px and 8.8 px apart, 7-11 percent of their own height, with no colour, crest or marking to help. It survives at full capture resolution, so it is not the software renderer. I picked all nine of my moves by reading the FEN out of the JS console; and since the HUD never prints state.lastMove, you also cannot tell what the engine just played.
